subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: The individual and the group (social identity theory, stereotypes)
Cultural origins of behaviour and cognition (culture, cultural dimensions)
Cultural influences on individual behaviour (enculturation, acculturation)
Ethical considerations and research methods in the sociocultural approach

questions.q: In social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner), the process of classifying people, including oneself, into groups is called:
questions.explain: SIT involves social categorization, social identification and social comparison; categorization is the first step of dividing the world into in-groups and out-groups.

questions.q: Tajfel's minimal group studies are significant because they suggest that:
options: Merely being assigned to a group, even a trivial one, can produce in-group favouritism
Discrimination requires real competition for resources
Group membership has no effect on behaviour
questions.explain: Even meaningless group assignments led participants to favour their in-group, supporting the idea that categorization alone drives bias.

questions.q: Within social identity theory, the motivation to view one's own group more favourably than others is known as:
questions.explain: People seek positive distinctiveness for the in-group through favourable social comparisons, enhancing self-esteem.

questions.q: Steele and Aronson's research on stereotype threat showed that:
options: Making a negative stereotype salient can impair the performance of stereotyped group members
questions.explain: When a relevant negative stereotype was activated, performance dropped, illustrating how stereotypes can affect behaviour.

questions.q: Participants randomly split by a coin toss still allocate more rewards to their own group. This finding is best explained by:
questions.explain: Favouritism towards an arbitrary in-group reflects social categorization and the pursuit of positive distinctiveness described by SIT.

questions.q: Hofstede's cultural dimension that contrasts prioritising personal goals with prioritising group loyalty is:
questions.explain: Individualism-collectivism captures whether a culture emphasises individual autonomy or group cohesion and obligations.

questions.q: A common criticism of using cultural dimensions such as Hofstede's is that they:
options: Can stereotype whole nations and overlook variation within a culture
Only apply to individuals, never groups
questions.explain: Dimension scores are broad national averages that risk overgeneralising and masking substantial within-culture diversity.

questions.q: Berry's cross-cultural study of conformity found the highest conformity in a collectivist, tightly organised society (the Temne) and the lowest in a more individualist society, the:
questions.explain: Berry reported low conformity among the individualist Inuit and high conformity among the collectivist, agrarian Temne.

questions.q: An 'etic' approach to studying behaviour involves:
options: Comparing cultures using constructs assumed to be universal
Studying a single culture entirely on its own terms
questions.explain: Etic research applies external, cross-cultural constructs, whereas emic research understands behaviour from within a specific culture.

questions.q: A researcher uses a Western depression questionnaire unchanged in another culture and assumes it measures the same construct. This risks:
questions.explain: Applying a culturally specific tool as if it were universal is an imposed etic and can misrepresent behaviour in the studied culture.

questions.q: Enculturation is the process by which a person:
options: Learns the norms and values of their own culture
Adapts to a completely new culture
questions.explain: Enculturation is the acquisition of one's own culture's norms, values and behaviours, often during childhood.

questions.q: Acculturation refers to:
options: The cultural and psychological change that results from contact with a different culture
questions.explain: Acculturation describes changes in behaviour and identity when individuals or groups come into sustained contact with another culture.

questions.q: Berry's model identifies four acculturation strategies: integration, assimilation, separation and:
questions.explain: Marginalization involves rejecting both the heritage and the host culture; the four strategies vary along maintenance of heritage and contact with the host culture.

questions.q: Acculturative stress is best described as:
options: Stress arising from the demands of adapting to a new culture
questions.explain: Adapting to new languages, norms and possible discrimination can produce acculturative stress, affecting wellbeing.

questions.q: A migrant who keeps strong ties to their heritage culture while also engaging fully with the host culture is using which acculturation strategy?
questions.explain: Integration combines maintenance of the heritage culture with participation in the host culture, and is often linked to better adjustment.

questions.q: Covert naturalistic observation raises ethical concerns mainly because participants:
options: Have not given informed consent and their privacy may be compromised
Know exactly what is being tested
questions.explain: Observing people without their knowledge conflicts with informed consent and privacy, so it must be justified and limited to public settings.

questions.q: A commonly cited strength of naturalistic observation is its:
questions.explain: Observing behaviour in real settings gives high ecological validity, though at the cost of control over confounding variables.

questions.q: Culture bias in psychological research occurs when:
options: Findings from one culture are wrongly assumed to apply to all cultures
A study has a large sample
questions.explain: Treating culturally specific findings as universal (e.g. through an imposed etic) is a form of culture bias.

questions.q: To reduce imposed-etic bias when studying a community, a researcher should:
options: Adapt measures to local meanings and involve members of that culture
questions.explain: Emic sensitivity, local collaboration and adapting instruments help ensure constructs are meaningful within the studied culture.

questions.q: Interviews, naturalistic observations and case studies used in the sociocultural approach are examples of:
questions.explain: These methods gather rich, in-depth data about meaning and context, characteristic of qualitative sociocultural research.

questions.q: Bandura's Bobo doll studies illustrate social cognitive theory by showing that behaviour can be acquired through:
options: Observation and imitation of a model
questions.explain: Children who watched an aggressive model imitated that aggression, supporting observational (social) learning.

questions.q: In social cognitive theory, vicarious reinforcement means a person is more likely to imitate a behaviour when they:
options: See a model being rewarded for it
questions.explain: Observing a model rewarded increases the likelihood of imitation, whereas seeing punishment reduces it.
